# Overview

## Question and hypothesis

**Central question of the project.** Do schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) share cell-type-specific
molecular alterations in the human prefrontal cortex, and could these changes reflect accelerated ageing and
affect neuronal and glial signalling networks?

**Question of this notebook (Q5).** *Do SCZ and BD show an accelerated-ageing-like transcriptomic profile in specific
neuronal or glial populations?*

**Hypothesis tested (H3).** In some cell populations, patients may have the transcriptomic profile of older controls,
in a way that is shared by the two disorders or specific to one of them.

## Why this question

Ageing is not a single process: it is described by a set of **hallmarks** [1], such as chronic inflammation, cellular
senescence or mitochondrial dysfunction, plus changes specific to the brain, such as the loss of myelin [2]. Whether
the brain ages faster in schizophrenia is **debated**: brain age estimated from MRI is older than chronological age in
patients [3], whereas an epigenetic clock measured on post-mortem cortex found no acceleration [4]. A recent
single-nucleus study of the orbitofrontal cortex found that genes changed with age and genes changed in psychiatric
disease (mostly schizophrenia) overlap and change in the same direction, and that patients have an older transcriptomic
age, but not an older epigenetic age [5]. We extend this question to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of the HBCC
cohort, compare **SCZ and BD** directly, and ask **which ageing hallmarks** are involved in each cell type.

## What we look for, and what we do not claim

**What we look for.** We do not test whether patients *age* faster, which cannot be shown with one sample per donor. We
ask whether, in some cell types, patients have the transcriptomic profile of **older controls**: for example, a
25-year-old patient whose microglia look like those of a 45-year-old control.

**How.** For each ageing hallmark, a **published gene signature** is scored per donor and cell type. The **controls**
define what is normal at each age; patients are compared with controls **of the same age**, and the difference is
expressed as an **apparent age gap** (in years). A complementary test, using all genes, checks whether the genes
changed by the disease (Q2) are the genes changed by age.

**What we will not claim.** A profile that resembles ageing does not mean that the disease causes ageing: treatments,
smoking, metabolic disorders and cause of death are other possible explanations, discussed as limits.

**Why signature scores.** Each hallmark is measured with `AddModuleScore()` [6], the Seurat function used in the
practicals to score gene signatures. It gives one interpretable number per nucleus for a named biological process, it
corrects for the general expression level of each nucleus, and it only needs published gene lists, which suits a
cohort with a limited number of controls per cell type.

## The scores used

Each hallmark is measured by a published signature, and only in the cell types where it makes biological sense, which
also limits the number of tests.

| Hallmark | Signature | Tested in | Ref. |
|----------|-----------|-----------|------|
| Cellular senescence | SenMayo | astrocytes, microglia | [1, 7] |
| Chronic inflammation ("inflammaging") | Hallmark Inflammatory Response; Hallmark TNFα signalling via NF-κB | astrocytes, microglia | [1, 2, 8] |
| Microglial ageing | genes rising / falling with age in human cortical microglia (GalatroAging) | microglia | [9] |
| Mitochondrial dysfunction | Hallmark Oxidative Phosphorylation | every cell type | [1, 2, 8] |
| Loss of myelin (brain-specific) | GO "ensheathment of neurons" (contains myelination) | oligodendrocytes, OPC | [2, 10] |
| Global transcriptomic age of the cell type | genes rising / falling with age in adult DLPFC (PsychAD lifespan atlas) | every cell type | [11] |

| Term | Meaning in this notebook |
|------|--------------------------|
| **Score** | one number per donor and cell type: how strongly the signature genes are expressed |
| **Validated score** | a score that follows age in our controls, in that cell type |
| **Ageing index** | for each cell type, the mean of its validated scores, oriented so that higher = older-looking: the **main measure** |
| **Apparent age gap** | how many years older (or younger) patients look than controls of the same age |

## Plan

| Step | What we do | Output |
|------|------------|--------|
| 1 | Check donors and choose the cell types analysed | tables |
| 2 | Prepare the signatures | tables |
| 3 | Score each nucleus, then average per donor and cell type | table |
| 4 | Keep only the scores that follow age in controls | F01 |
| 5 | Build the ageing index of each cell type | table |
| 6 | Do patients look older than controls of the same age? SCZ, BD, and SCZ vs BD | F02, F03, F04, F05 |

| 8 | Synthesis | summary table |

# Setup

| Package | Used for |
|---------|----------|
| `Seurat` | Seurat object, `AddModuleScore()` (seen in the practicals) |
| `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `ggplot2` | tables and figures |

```{r setup}
the.seed <- 42          # AddModuleScore draws control genes at random: a fixed seed makes it reproducible
set.seed(the.seed)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Seurat)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})

# Reusable functions, kept outside the notebook so the code below stays readable
source("R/utils_genesets.R")
source("R/utils_aging_scores.R")
source("R/utils_figures.R")     # common figure style, colours and saving (shared with the other notebooks)
```

All the choices are gathered in one place, so the analysis can be re-run with other values.

| Parameter | Value | Why |
|-----------|-------|-----|
| `subclass_column` / `class_column` | `cell_subclass` / `cell_class` | shared rule of the project: subclasses, merged into their class when too rare |
| `min_cells` | 20 nuclei | a donor mean computed on fewer nuclei is too noisy (shared rule) |
| `min_donors` | 10 donors per group | below this, a group is too small to compare (shared rule) |
| `min_age` | 20 years | adult donors only (shared rule): younger brains are still developing |
| `min_genes` | 5 genes | a signature with fewer genes present in the data is not reliable |
| `covariates` | sex, PMI | known to change expression; age and diagnosis are in the models by design |
| `n_perm` | 200 | number of permutations of the concordance test (Step 7) |
| `alpha` | 0.05 | threshold on the adjusted p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg) |

`AddModuleScore()` is used with its default of 100 control genes per signature gene: more control genes give a more
stable background estimate.

```{r parameters}
# Inputs
seurat_path   <- "../01_DATA/processed/hbcc_seurat_preprocessed.rds"
de_path       <- "../03_RESULTS/Q2_pseudobulk_DE/de_results_all.csv"   # Q2 results, for Step 7
geneset_dir   <- "../01_DATA/genesets"   # one CSV per signature (gs_name, gene_symbol), see its README.md
signature_files <- c("Q5_senmayo.csv", "Q5_inflammatory_response.csv", "Q5_tnfa_nfkb.csv",
                     "Q5_microglia_ageing_galatro.csv", "Q5_oxphos.csv", "Q5_myelination.csv")
lifespan_path <- file.path(geneset_dir, "Q5_lifespan_ageing.csv")

# Outputs
out_dir <- "../03_RESULTS/Q5_aging"
fig_dir <- "../04_FIGURES/Q5"
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Analysis choices
subclass_column <- "cell_subclass"
class_column    <- "cell_class"
min_cells       <- 20
min_donors      <- 10
min_age         <- 20
min_genes       <- 5
covariates      <- c("sex", "pmi")
n_perm          <- 200
alpha           <- 0.05
key_celltypes   <- c("Micro", "Astro", "Oligo")   # shown in Figure F03; replace with the cell types highlighted in Q1

# In which cell classes each signature is tested ("all" = every cell type)
signature_scope <- list(
  SenMayo               = c("Astro", "Micro"),
  Inflammatory_Response = c("Astro", "Micro"),
  TNFa_NFkB             = c("Astro", "Micro"),
  Microglia_AgingUp     = "Micro",
  Microglia_AgingDown   = "Micro",
  OxPhos                = "all",
  Myelination           = c("Oligo", "OPC"),
  Lifespan_AgingUp      = "all",
  Lifespan_AgingDown    = "all"
)

col_dx <- c(CTRL = "grey40", col_disease[c("SCZ", "BD")])
lab_dx <- c(SCZ = "SCZ vs controls", BD = "BD vs controls", SCZ_vs_BD = "SCZ vs BD (direct)")

# Diverging scale for ageing shifts: orange = older-looking, purple = younger-looking
scale_fill_shift <- function(lim, name) {
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#5e3c99", mid = "white", high = "#e66101", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-lim, lim), name = name)
}
```

# Step 1 – Donors and cell types

**What we do and why.** In a cross-sectional study, the main risk is **confounding**: if patients were younger or
older than controls, age and diagnosis would be mixed up. We first check that the groups are comparable, then choose
the cell types analysed with the shared rule of the project.

```{r load}
sobj <- readRDS(seurat_path)

missing_cols <- setdiff(c(META_REQUIRED_COLUMNS, subclass_column, class_column), colnames(sobj@meta.data))
if (length(missing_cols) > 0) stop("Missing metadata columns: ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "))

# AddModuleScore uses the log-normalised "data" layer; layers must be joined (one layer per assay)
if (length(Layers(sobj, search = "data")) > 1) sobj <- JoinLayers(sobj)

donor_meta <- sobj@meta.data |>
  distinct(donor_id, diagnosis, age, sex, pmi) |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("CTRL", "SCZ", "BD")))

# Adult donors only (should already be done in preprocessing: this is a safety check)
n_young <- sum(donor_meta$age < min_age)
if (n_young > 0) {
  cat("Note:", n_young, "donors under", min_age, "years removed.\n")
  donor_meta <- filter(donor_meta, age >= min_age)
  sobj <- subset(sobj, cells = colnames(sobj)[sobj$donor_id %in% donor_meta$donor_id])
}

donor_meta |>
  group_by(diagnosis) |>
  summarise(n_donors   = n(),
            age_median = median(age),
            age_range  = paste(min(age), "-", max(age)),
            pct_female = round(100 * mean(sex == "female")),
            pmi_median = median(pmi, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

kruskal.test(age ~ diagnosis, data = donor_meta)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
One row per group: number of donors, median and range of age at death, percentage of women, median post-mortem interval
(PMI). The Kruskal–Wallis test checks whether the age distributions differ between groups (without assuming a normal
distribution). The same information is in Table 1 of the report (preprocessing).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Do the three groups cover the same age range? Patients often die younger: the models below compare them with
  controls **of the same age**, but the oldest ages will be represented mostly by controls.
- Are sex and PMI balanced? An imbalance is handled by the covariates, but must be reported.
- If the metadata contain metabolic disorders (for example diabetes), are they more frequent in patients? See the
  limits.
:::

**Which cell types are analysed.** A subclass is analysed on its own if at least `r min_donors` donors of **each** group
have at least `r min_cells` nuclei of it. Otherwise its nuclei are pooled with the other rare subclasses of the same
class (unit `<class>_other`), or with the whole class if no subclass of that class is kept.

```{r units}
units <- assign_analysis_units(sobj@meta.data, subclass_column, class_column,
                               min_cells = min_cells, min_donors = min_donors)
sobj$analysis_unit <- units$unit
unit_class <- setNames(units$decision$class, units$decision$unit)   # class of each analysis unit
units$decision
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
One row per subclass: number of donors with at least `r min_cells` nuclei of it, in each group, and the analysis unit
it goes to (`unit`). `enough_donors = FALSE`: the subclass is pooled with others.
:::

# Step 2 – The signatures

**What we do and why.** We load the published signatures listed in the overview. The lifespan signatures come from the
PsychAD lifespan atlas [11], which studied the same brain region with the same technique: for each subclass, the genes
that change with age **in adulthood** (age groups 20–39, 40–59 and ≥ 60 years; childhood excluded), split into genes
that rise and genes that fall with age (see `01_DATA/genesets/README.md`).

```{r signatures}
# One file per signature; myelination is the GO term "ensheathment of neurons" (GO:0007272), which contains
# myelination (GO:0042552)
common_sets <- bind_rows(lapply(file.path(geneset_dir, signature_files), read_geneset_file))
common_signatures <- term2gene_to_list(common_sets)
short_names <- c(SAUL_SEN_MAYO = "SenMayo", SENMAYO = "SenMayo",
                 HALLMARK_INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE = "Inflammatory_Response",
                 HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB = "TNFa_NFkB",
                 HALLMARK_OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION = "OxPhos",
                 GOBP_ENSHEATHMENT_OF_NEURONS = "Myelination",
                 GALATRO_AGING_UP = "Microglia_AgingUp", GALATRO_AGING_DOWN = "Microglia_AgingDown")
names(common_signatures) <- ifelse(names(common_signatures) %in% names(short_names),
                                   short_names[names(common_signatures)], names(common_signatures))

# Lifespan atlas genes: gs_name AGING_UP_<cell type> / AGING_DOWN_<cell type>
lifespan_sets <- read_geneset_file(lifespan_path)
if (is.null(lifespan_sets)) cat("Note: lifespan file not found, the lifespan signatures are skipped.\n")

# Signatures used for one analysis unit, following signature_scope
signatures_for_unit <- function(unit) {
  cl <- unit_class[[unit]]
  in_scope <- function(sig) any(signature_scope[[sig]] %in% c("all", cl))
  sigs <- common_signatures[vapply(names(common_signatures), in_scope, logical(1))]
  if (!is.null(lifespan_sets)) {
    for (dir in c("UP", "DOWN")) {
      # the lifespan atlas may be annotated at subclass or class level: try the unit first, then its class
      for (key in c(unit, cl)) {
        genes <- lifespan_sets$gene_symbol[lifespan_sets$gs_name == paste0("AGING_", dir, "_", key)]
        if (length(genes) > 0) {
          sigs[[paste0("Lifespan_Aging", ifelse(dir == "UP", "Up", "Down"))]] <- genes
          break
        }
      }
    }
  }
  sigs
}

# Coverage: how many genes of each signature are in our data?
geneset_coverage(common_signatures, rownames(sobj))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
`n_genes` = size of the signature; `n_present` = genes found in our data; `fraction_present` = their ratio. Missing genes
are usually not expressed in the cortex.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Is every signature at least ~70 % covered? A poorly covered signature should be interpreted with caution or dropped.
:::

**Do the signatures overlap?** If two signatures share most of their genes, they are not independent evidence.

```{r signature-overlap}
sig_names <- names(common_signatures)
expand.grid(sig_a = sig_names, sig_b = sig_names, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  filter(sig_a < sig_b) |>
  mutate(shared_genes = mapply(function(a, b) length(intersect(common_signatures[[a]], common_signatures[[b]])), sig_a, sig_b),
         jaccard = mapply(function(a, b) {
           ga <- common_signatures[[a]]; gb <- common_signatures[[b]]
           round(length(intersect(ga, gb)) / length(union(ga, gb)), 2)
         }, sig_a, sig_b)) |>
  arrange(desc(jaccard))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
One row per pair of signatures: number of shared genes and Jaccard index (shared genes / all genes of the two
signatures; 0 = nothing in common, 1 = identical).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Do the inflammation signatures and SenMayo overlap strongly? If yes, a result found with all of them is less
  independent than it looks: say so in the report.
:::

# Step 3 – Scores per donor and cell type

**How a score is computed.** `AddModuleScore()` takes, for each nucleus, the mean expression of the signature genes and
subtracts the mean expression of random "control" genes with a similar expression level. A positive score means that
the signature genes are higher than comparable genes in that nucleus; using control genes of the same level removes the
effect of sequencing depth.

**Why one score per donor.** Nuclei of the same donor are not independent: they share the donor's genetics, age,
treatment and post-mortem conditions. Testing nuclei as if they were independent would give many false positives
(pseudoreplication, the same reason Q2 uses pseudobulk). The **donor** is the statistical unit: scores are averaged per
donor and cell type (donors with fewer than `r min_cells` nuclei are left out for that cell type), then expressed as
**z-scores relative to the controls** (1 unit = 1 standard deviation of the controls), so all scores are on the same
scale. The object is processed one cell type at a time to limit memory use; the effect of age on every gene in controls,
used in Step 7, is computed in the same loop.

```{r scoring, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(file.mtime(seurat_path), file.mtime(geneset_dir), file.mtime(lifespan_path))}
analysis_units    <- sort(unique(sobj$analysis_unit))
donor_scores_list <- list()
age_fits          <- list()   # effect of age on all genes in controls, per cell type (Step 7)

for (u in analysis_units) {
  sobj_u <- subset(sobj, cells = colnames(sobj)[sobj$analysis_unit == u])

  cell_scores <- score_one_celltype(sobj_u, signatures_for_unit(u), seed = the.seed, min_genes = min_genes)
  if (!is.null(cell_scores)) {
    donor_scores_list[[u]] <- aggregate_by_donor(cell_scores, sobj_u$donor_id, u, min_cells = min_cells)
  }
  age_fits[[u]] <- age_effects_in_controls(sobj_u, donor_meta, covariates = covariates, min_donors = min_donors)
  rm(sobj_u); invisible(gc())
}

donor_scores <- bind_rows(donor_scores_list) |>
  left_join(donor_meta, by = "donor_id") |>
  standardize_by_controls()

# Signatures scored in each cell type
donor_scores |>
  distinct(cell_type, signature) |>
  group_by(cell_type) |>
  summarise(signatures = paste(sort(signature), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
For each cell type, the signatures that were scored, following `signature_scope`. A signature can be missing if fewer
than `r min_genes` of its genes are in the data.
:::

# Step 4 – Which scores really follow age?

**What we do and why.** A score is only an ageing measure if it changes with age in **healthy** donors. For each cell
type and signature, we compute the Spearman correlation between the score and age in controls (rank-based, so robust to
extreme values). A score is **validated** if this correlation is significant after correction; its **direction** is kept
(+1 if it rises with age, −1 if it falls), so that every score can be read as "older-looking" afterwards.

The lifespan atlas was built partly on HBCC controls, very probably ours [11]: its signatures are expected to follow age
in our controls. This is not independent evidence, but it is not a problem for the question, which compares
**patients** with controls.

```{r validation}
validation <- validate_in_controls(donor_scores, min_donors = min_donors)
write.csv(validation, file.path(out_dir, "validation_controls.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

valid_pairs <- validation |>
  filter(p_adj < alpha) |>
  transmute(cell_type, signature, age_direction = sign(rho))
validation |> mutate(rho = round(rho, 2), validated = p_adj < alpha)
```

```{r fig-F01, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
p_F01 <- ggplot(validation, aes(signature, cell_type, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(p_adj < alpha, "*", "")), size = 6, vjust = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_shift(1, "Spearman rho\n(score vs age)") +
  labs(x = "Signature", y = "Cell type",
       title = "Correlation of each ageing score with age in controls",
       subtitle = paste0("Control donors only; * adjusted p < ", alpha, " (validated score). Grey cell: signature not tested there"),
       caption = "Orange: the score rises with age; purple: it decreases with age.") +
  theme_project() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right",
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"))
p_F01
save_figure(p_F01, "Q5_F01_validation_controls", fig_dir, width = 9, height = 5)
```

**Figure Q5-F01 – Validation of the ageing scores in controls.** Spearman correlation between each signature score
(donor mean, z-score) and age at death, in control donors, per cell type. \* Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05.
Signatures are only tested in the cell types where they are biologically relevant (grey cells: not tested).

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each cell is a score in a cell type. Orange = the score rises with age, purple = it falls with age, white = no link with
age. Only cells with a star are used as ageing measures in the rest of the notebook.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which scores are validated? We expect senescence and inflammation to rise in microglia and astrocytes, and
  myelination to fall in oligodendrocytes.
- Does OxPhos fall with age in neurons, as expected from mitochondrial decline?
- A cell type with no validated score cannot be tested for an ageing-like profile.
:::

# Step 5 – The ageing index of each cell type

**What we do and why.** Rather than testing every signature separately, we summarise each cell type by one **ageing
index**: the mean of its validated scores, each one oriented so that higher always means older-looking (a falling score,
such as myelination, is multiplied by −1). The index is then re-expressed as a z-score relative to the controls. It is
the **main test** of this notebook: one index per cell type, so few tests and a light multiple-testing correction. The
individual signatures are kept as a detailed analysis, to see which hallmark drives an effect. The index is chosen on
controls only and never looks at the diagnosis, so it does not favour a difference between patients and controls.

```{r aging-index}
donor_scores <- add_aging_index(donor_scores, valid_pairs)
write.csv(donor_scores, file.path(out_dir, "donor_scores.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Components of the index in each cell type
valid_pairs |>
  mutate(component = paste0(signature, ifelse(age_direction > 0, " (+)", " (-)"))) |>
  group_by(cell_type) |>
  summarise(n_signatures = n(), index_components = paste(component, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
For each cell type, the validated signatures averaged into its ageing index. `(+)` = rises with age, `(-)` = falls with
age and is inverted in the index. Cell types without any validated signature have no index.
:::

# Step 6 – Do patients look older than controls of the same age?

## Two patterns, and the apparent age gap

**What we do and why.** An ageing-like profile can take two forms, tested with two linear models (one per cell type):

| Model | Formula | What is tested | Meaning if significant |
|-------|---------|----------------|------------------------|
| **Offset** | `score ~ age + diagnosis + sex + pmi` | `diagnosis` | patients look older than controls **of the same age**, at every age |
| **Slope** | `score ~ age * diagnosis + sex + pmi` | `age:diagnosis` | the score changes **faster with age** in patients |

Putting age in the model compares patients and controls **of the same age**. For each model we test SCZ vs controls, BD
vs controls, and **SCZ vs BD directly** (difference of the two effects in the same model): an effect seen in one
disease only is called specific only if the direct test is significant.

**Apparent age gap.** In the offset model, the disease effect divided by the effect of one year of age gives how many
**years** older (or younger) patients look than controls of the same age, with a 95 % confidence interval (delta
method). It is only meaningful for scores that follow age clearly in controls, which is the case of the ageing index by
construction.

```{r fig-F02, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
concept <- expand.grid(age = seq(20, 90, 5), group = c("Controls", "Patients"),
                       model = c("Offset: older at every age", "Slope: faster change with age"))
concept$score <- with(concept, 0.03 * (age - 20) +
  ifelse(group == "Patients" & model == "Offset: older at every age", 0.6, 0) +
  ifelse(group == "Patients" & model == "Slope: faster change with age", 0.02 * (age - 20), 0))

p_F02 <- ggplot(concept, aes(age, score, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(data = data.frame(model = factor("Offset: older at every age", levels = levels(concept$model))),
               aes(x = 40, xend = 60, y = 1.2, yend = 1.2), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Controls = "grey40", Patients = "#a88600"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Age at death (years)", y = "Ageing score",
       title = "Two patterns of an ageing-like profile",
       subtitle = "Schematic illustration (invented data)",
       caption = "Offset: a 40-year-old patient has the score of a 60-year-old control (dotted line = apparent age gap of 20 years).") +
  theme_project()
p_F02
save_figure(p_F02, "Q5_F02_offset_slope_schema", fig_dir, width = 9, height = 4)
```

**Figure Q5-F02 – Two patterns of an ageing-like profile (schematic).** Offset model (left): patients have a higher
ageing score than controls of the same age, at every age; the horizontal distance between the two lines is the apparent
age gap. Slope model (right): the score rises faster with age in patients. Invented data.

```{r models}
model_data <- donor_scores |>
  filter(!is.na(score_z)) |>
  mutate(sex = factor(sex))

models <- fit_disease_models(model_data, covariates = covariates, min_donors_per_group = min_donors) |>
  adjust_by_family() |>
  left_join(valid_pairs, by = c("cell_type", "signature")) |>
  mutate(validated = signature == "Ageing_index" | !is.na(age_direction),
         age_direction = ifelse(signature == "Ageing_index", 1, coalesce(age_direction, 1)),
         # > 0 = shifted towards an older profile (for SCZ vs BD: SCZ older-looking than BD)
         aging_shift = estimate * age_direction,
         lower = pmin(estimate - 1.96 * std_error, estimate + 1.96 * std_error) * age_direction,
         upper = pmax(estimate - 1.96 * std_error, estimate + 1.96 * std_error) * age_direction,
         years_lower = years - 1.96 * years_se,
         years_upper = years + 1.96 * years_se,
         comparison = factor(comparison, levels = c("SCZ", "BD", "SCZ_vs_BD")))
write.csv(models, file.path(out_dir, "disease_models.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Main test: ageing index, offset model
models |>
  filter(signature == "Ageing_index", model == "offset") |>
  select(cell_type, comparison, n_CTRL, n_SCZ, n_BD, aging_shift, years, years_lower, years_upper, p_adj) |>
  mutate(across(c(aging_shift, years, years_lower, years_upper), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Main test: one row per cell type and comparison. `aging_shift` = difference between patients and controls of the same
age, in control standard deviations; `years` = the same difference expressed as an apparent age gap, with its 95 %
confidence interval (`years_lower`, `years_upper`); `p_adj` = adjusted p-value. For `SCZ_vs_BD`, positive values mean SCZ
looks older than BD.
:::

## The main result: the ageing index

```{r fig-F03, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
index_data <- model_data |>
  filter(signature == "Ageing_index", cell_type %in% key_celltypes)

if (nrow(index_data) > 0) {
  p_F03 <- ggplot(index_data, aes(age, score_z, colour = diagnosis)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~ cell_type) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = col_dx, name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Age at death (years)", y = "Ageing index\n(z-score vs controls)",
         title = "Ageing index versus age, per group",
         subtitle = "One dot per donor; lines = linear fit per group",
         caption = "Higher index = older-looking profile. Raw fits, not adjusted for sex and PMI (the models are).") +
    theme_project()
  print(p_F03)
  save_figure(p_F03, "Q5_F03_index_vs_age", fig_dir, width = 10, height = 4.5)
}
```

**Figure Q5-F03 – Ageing index versus age in key cell types.** Ageing index (mean of the validated ageing scores of the
cell type, oriented towards an older profile, z-score relative to controls) as a function of age at death, for controls
(grey), SCZ (blue) and BD (red). Each dot is a donor; lines are linear fits per group.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
In controls, the grey line goes up: this is what "ageing index" means. A coloured line **above and parallel** to the
grey one means patients look older at every age (offset); a **steeper** coloured line means a faster change with age
(slope).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which pattern (offset, slope, none) do we see for SCZ and BD in each cell type?
- Are a few extreme donors driving the lines? If so, mention it.
:::

```{r fig-F04, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
forest <- models |>
  filter(signature == "Ageing_index", model == "offset")

if (nrow(forest) > 0) {
  direct_lab <- forest |>
    filter(comparison == "SCZ_vs_BD") |>
    mutate(label = paste0("SCZ vs BD: ", sprintf("%+.1f", years), " y, adj. p = ", signif(p_adj, 2)))
  x_text <- max(forest$years_upper[forest$comparison != "SCZ_vs_BD"], na.rm = TRUE) + 1

  p_F04 <- forest |>
    filter(comparison != "SCZ_vs_BD") |>
    ggplot(aes(years, cell_type, colour = comparison, group = comparison)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = years_lower, xmax = years_upper), width = 0.25, orientation = "y",
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = p_adj < alpha), size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    geom_text(data = direct_lab, aes(x = x_text, y = cell_type, label = label),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey25") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(SCZ = col_disease[["SCZ"]], BD = col_disease[["BD"]]),
                        labels = lab_dx, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16),
                       labels = c(`FALSE` = "not significant", `TRUE` = paste0("adjusted p < ", alpha)), name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.45))) +
    labs(x = "Apparent age gap vs controls of the same age (years, 95% CI)",
         y = "Cell type",
         title = "Apparent age gap of the ageing index in patients",
         subtitle = "Offset model adjusted for age, sex and PMI; right: direct SCZ vs BD comparison",
         caption = "Right of the dashed line: patients look older than controls of the same age. 'SCZ vs BD' > 0: SCZ older-looking than BD.") +
    theme_project()
  print(p_F04)
  save_figure(p_F04, "Q5_F04_index_forest", fig_dir, width = 10, height = 6)
}
```

**Figure Q5-F04 – Apparent age gap of SCZ and BD patients compared with controls of the same age.** Difference in
ageing index between patients and controls (offset linear model adjusted for age, sex and PMI), expressed in years of
age (disease effect divided by the effect of one year of age, 95 % confidence interval by the delta method), for SCZ
(blue) and BD (red), in the cell types that have at least one validated ageing score. Filled dots: Benjamini–Hochberg
adjusted p < 0.05. The text on the right gives the direct SCZ vs BD comparison.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
One line per cell type. A dot at +10 means patients look 10 years older than controls of the same age; the bar is the
uncertainty. Filled dots are significant. The text on the right says whether SCZ and BD differ from each other: only then
can an effect be called specific to one disease.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- In which cell types do SCZ and BD look older, and by how many years?
- Is the effect shared (both filled, same side) or specific (only one filled **and** a significant direct test)?
- A wide bar that crosses 0 means "no conclusion" (not enough donors), not "no ageing-like profile".
:::

## Which hallmark drives the effect?

**What we do and why.** For the cell types where the index shifts, the individual signatures show which hallmark
(senescence, inflammation, mitochondria, myelin...) carries the effect. These are secondary tests, corrected separately.

```{r fig-F05, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
detail <- models |>
  filter(signature != "Ageing_index", model == "offset") |>
  mutate(label = case_when(p_adj < alpha & validated ~ "*",
                           p_adj < alpha ~ "+",
                           TRUE ~ ""))

if (nrow(detail) > 0) {
  lim_d <- max(abs(detail$aging_shift), na.rm = TRUE)
  p_F05 <- ggplot(detail, aes(signature, cell_type, fill = aging_shift)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 5, vjust = 0.75) +
    facet_wrap(~ comparison, labeller = as_labeller(lab_dx)) +
    scale_fill_shift(lim_d, "Shift towards\nolder profile\n(control SD)") +
    labs(x = "Signature", y = "Cell type",
         title = "Ageing shift of each signature in patients",
         subtitle = paste0("Offset model; * adjusted p < ", alpha, " and score validated in controls; + adjusted p < ", alpha, " only"),
         caption = "Orange: older-looking (right panel: SCZ older-looking than BD). Grey cell: signature not tested there.") +
    theme_project() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right",
          panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"))
  print(p_F05)
  save_figure(p_F05, "Q5_F05_signatures_heatmap", fig_dir, width = 11, height = 5)
}
```

**Figure Q5-F05 – Ageing shift of each signature.** Difference between patients and controls of the same age (offset
linear model adjusted for sex and PMI), oriented so that positive values mean an older-looking profile, for each
signature and cell type, in SCZ, BD and SCZ vs BD. \* Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05 and score validated in
controls; + adjusted p < 0.05 for a score that does not follow age in controls. Grey cells: signature not tested in
that cell type.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each cell is one signature in one cell type. Orange = patients look older on that hallmark. A star means the hallmark is
a validated ageing measure **and** the effect is significant: evidence for H3. A `+` means a significant disease effect on
a process that does not follow age in controls: interesting, but not an ageing-like effect.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- In the cell types where the index shifts (F04), which hallmarks carry the effect?
- If only the inflammation signatures move, it is an inflammatory effect of the disease (or of treatments), rather than
  a broad ageing-like profile: Step 7 helps to tell the two apart.
:::

## Do patients change faster with age? (slope model)

```{r slope}
models |>
  filter(model == "slope", signature == "Ageing_index") |>
  select(cell_type, comparison, aging_shift, lower, upper, p_adj) |>
  mutate(across(c(aging_shift, lower, upper), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
`aging_shift` is here the **extra change of the index per year of age** in patients compared with controls (for
`SCZ_vs_BD`: in SCZ compared with BD). Detecting a difference of slope needs many donors across a wide age range, so
this test is often not significant; it is reported as a table, and as a figure only if a result is found.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- An offset without a slope effect means patients look older at every age, without diverging further with age.
:::

# Step 7 – Are the genes changed by the disease the genes changed by age?

**What we do and why.** The scores look at chosen gene lists. This test, close to the approach of [5], looks at
**all genes**, without any list: in each
cell type, it compares the effect of age on each gene (in controls) with the effect of the disease on the same gene (Q2,
DESeq2 Wald statistic). If the genes that rise with age also rise in the disease, and the genes that fall with age also
fall, the correlation is positive: the disease profile **resembles** the ageing profile. It helps to tell a broad
ageing-like profile (high correlation) from a targeted effect, for example on inflammation only (low correlation).

**How.** The effect of age is a linear model per gene on the pseudobulk of the controls (`expression ~ age + sex + pmi`),
fitted for all genes at once. The Spearman correlation with the Q2 statistic is computed over all genes tested in both.
To know which correlations can arise by chance, the ages of the controls are shuffled `r n_perm` times (permutation test).
This needs the Q2 cell types to have the same names as the analysis units of this notebook.

```{r concordance, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(file.mtime(seurat_path), file.mtime(de_path))}
concordance <- NULL
if (file.exists(de_path)) {
  de <- read.csv(de_path)
  concordance <- bind_rows(lapply(names(age_fits), function(u) {
    if (is.null(age_fits[[u]])) return(NULL)
    bind_rows(lapply(c(SCZ = "SCZ_vs_CTRL", BD = "BD_vs_CTRL"), function(co) {
      d <- de[de$cell_type == u & de$contrast == co & !is.na(de$stat), ]
      if (nrow(d) == 0) return(NULL)
      res <- age_disease_concordance(age_fits[[u]], setNames(d$stat, d$gene), n_perm = n_perm, seed = the.seed)
      if (is.null(res)) return(NULL)
      cbind(cell_type = u, comparison = sub("_vs_CTRL", "", co), res)
    }))
  }))
  if (nrow(concordance) > 0) {
    concordance$p_adj <- p.adjust(concordance$p_perm, method = "BH")
    write.csv(concordance, file.path(out_dir, "age_disease_concordance.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  } else {
    cat("Note: no cell type in common between Q2 and Q5: the concordance test is skipped.\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("Note: Q2 table not found, the concordance test is skipped.\n")
}
if (!is.null(concordance) && nrow(concordance) > 0) mutate(concordance, across(c(rho, null_low, null_high), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r fig-F06, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
if (!is.null(concordance) && nrow(concordance) > 0) {
  p_F06 <- concordance |>
    mutate(comparison = factor(comparison, levels = c("SCZ", "BD"))) |>
    ggplot(aes(rho, cell_type, colour = comparison, group = comparison)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = null_low, xmax = null_high), width = 0.3, orientation = "y", colour = "grey70",
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = p_adj < alpha), size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(SCZ = col_disease[["SCZ"]], BD = col_disease[["BD"]]),
                        labels = lab_dx, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16),
                       labels = c(`FALSE` = "not significant", `TRUE` = paste0("adjusted p < ", alpha)), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Correlation between the age effect and the disease effect\n(Spearman rho, all genes)",
         y = "Cell type",
         title = "Concordance between the effects of age and of the disease on all genes",
         subtitle = paste0("Age effect in controls vs disease effect (Q2); grey bar: range expected by chance (", n_perm, " permutations)"),
         caption = "Positive: the genes changed by the disease change in the same direction as with age.") +
    theme_project()
  print(p_F06)
  save_figure(p_F06, "Q5_F06_age_disease_concordance", fig_dir, width = 9, height = 5)
}
```

**Figure Q5-F06 – Concordance between the effects of age and of the disease on gene expression.** For each cell type,
Spearman correlation, over all genes tested in both analyses, between the effect of age in controls (t statistic of age
in a pseudobulk linear model adjusted for sex and PMI) and the effect of the disease (DESeq2 Wald statistic, Q2), for
SCZ (blue) and BD (red). Grey bars: 95 % range of the correlation expected by chance (ages permuted among controls).
Filled dots: Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted permutation p < 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
A dot to the right of the grey bar means that the disease moves genes in the same direction as age, more than expected
by chance: the disease profile resembles the ageing profile in that cell type. A dot inside the grey bar means no such
resemblance.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- In which cell types is the concordance positive? Are they the same as in F04? Agreement between the two approaches is
  the strongest argument for an ageing-like profile.
- Is the concordance similar in SCZ and BD (shared) or only in one disease?
:::

## Complementary test: do age and disease change the same genes? (Fisher)

**What we do and why.** The correlation above uses all genes, without any threshold. Here we ask a simpler question,
as in [5]: among the genes **significantly** changed, are the genes changed with age and the genes changed in the disease
the **same genes**, more often than by chance? The answer is a count (for example "120 genes in common, 3 times more than
expected"), easy to report in the text and on a slide.

**How.** In each cell type, every gene tested in both analyses is placed in a 2 × 2 table:

| | changed in the disease (Q2, adjusted p < `r alpha`) | not changed |
|---|---|---|
| **changed with age** (controls, adjusted p < `r alpha`) | a | b |
| **not changed with age** | c | d |

- The **Fisher exact test** (one-sided) asks whether box *a* is larger than expected by chance. It compares counts in a
  table, not means; it is exact, so it stays valid when a box contains few genes. The **odds ratio** gives the size of
  the effect: 1 = overlap expected by chance, 3 = three times more overlap than by chance.
- Among the genes of box *a*, a **binomial test** checks whether more than half change **in the same direction** with
  age and with the disease (50 % = chance). An overlap in opposite directions would not mean an ageing-like profile.

**Why it does not replace the correlation.** The Fisher test assumes that genes are independent, which is not true
(genes of the same pathway change together): its p-values are therefore optimistic. It also depends on the thresholds.
The correlation with permutations (F06) keeps the correlation between genes and stays the main test; the Fisher test
backs it up with a readable count.

```{r overlap, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=list(file.mtime(seurat_path), file.mtime(de_path))}
overlap <- NULL
if (file.exists(de_path)) {
  overlap <- bind_rows(lapply(names(age_fits), function(u) {
    if (is.null(age_fits[[u]])) return(NULL)
    bind_rows(lapply(c(SCZ = "SCZ_vs_CTRL", BD = "BD_vs_CTRL"), function(co) {
      d <- de[de$cell_type == u & de$contrast == co, ]
      if (nrow(d) == 0) return(NULL)
      res <- age_disease_overlap(age_fits[[u]], setNames(d$stat, d$gene), setNames(d$padj, d$gene), alpha = alpha)
      if (is.null(res)) return(NULL)
      cbind(cell_type = u, comparison = sub("_vs_CTRL", "", co), res)
    }))
  }))
  if (nrow(overlap) > 0) {
    overlap$p_adj_fisher    <- p.adjust(overlap$p_fisher, method = "BH")
    overlap$p_adj_direction <- p.adjust(overlap$p_direction, method = "BH")
    write.csv(overlap, file.path(out_dir, "age_disease_overlap_fisher.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
    overlap |>
      transmute(cell_type, comparison, n_age, n_disease, n_both, expected_both,
                odds_ratio = round(odds_ratio, 2), p_adj_fisher = signif(p_adj_fisher, 2),
                pct_same_direction, p_adj_direction = signif(p_adj_direction, 2))
  }
}
```

**Table – Overlap between age-associated and disease-associated genes.** `n_age`, `n_disease`: genes significant with
age in controls and in the disease (Q2); `n_both`: genes significant in both; `expected_both`: number expected by
chance; `odds_ratio` and `p_adj_fisher`: one-sided Fisher exact test; `pct_same_direction` and `p_adj_direction`:
percentage of common genes changed in the same direction, binomial test against 50 %. Benjamini–Hochberg correction
over cell types and diseases. If very few genes are significant with age (few controls), the test has little power:
a non-significant result then means "not testable", not "no overlap".

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- In which cell types is the overlap larger than expected (odds ratio > 1, adjusted p < 0.05)? Are they the cell types
  with a positive correlation in F06?
- Do most common genes change in the same direction? For comparison, more than 75 % did in [5].
:::

# Synthesis: answer to Q5

**Decision grid.** We speak of an **accelerated-ageing-like profile** in a cell type only if: (1) at least one score
follows age in controls (F01); (2) the ageing index of patients is shifted towards an older profile at equal age (F04);
(3) the shift is carried by more than the inflammation signatures alone (F05); (4) the concordance test is positive in
the same cell type (F06), backed by the overlap of significant genes in the same direction (Fisher table). A specific effect also needs a significant direct SCZ vs BD test.

::: {.callout-important title="Summary table [to fill after the analysis]"}
| Element | Result | Figure |
|---------|--------|--------|
| Scores that follow age in controls (cell types) | | F01 |
| Cell types older-looking in SCZ, apparent age gap (years) | | F03, F04 |
| Cell types older-looking in BD, apparent age gap (years) | | F03, F04 |
| Shared or specific (direct SCZ vs BD test) | | F04 |
| Hallmarks driving the effect | | F05 |
| Concordance of disease and age effects (all genes) | | F06 |
| Overlap of significant genes, same direction (Fisher) | | table, Step 7 |
| Faster change with age (slope)? | | table |
| **Is H3 supported, according to the decision grid?** | | |
:::

**Links with the other questions.**

- **Q3**: inflammation, mitochondrial and myelination pathways found in Q3 should be consistent with the scores here.
  Q3 compares patients and controls; Q5 adds the **age** dimension.
- **Q4**: altered intercellular communication is also a hallmark of ageing [1]; Q4 can compare young and old controls.
- **Q1**: a change in the proportion of a cell type can be linked to its ageing index.

# Limits to discuss in the report

- **Cross-sectional design.** Each donor is seen once: an ageing-like profile is inferred between donors, not followed
  over time.
- **Not a proof of ageing.** A profile that resembles ageing can have other causes; we only describe a resemblance.
- **Treatments and metabolic disorders.** Antipsychotics, lithium and smoking change inflammation, metabolic and myelin
  genes. Donors with metabolic disorders (for example diabetes) are kept, as in Lee et al. [12]; these disorders are more
  frequent in patients (partly because of antipsychotics), and are themselves associated with accelerated ageing. If the
  information is in the metadata, a sensitivity analysis without these donors should be run; otherwise it is a limit.
- **Survival bias and cause of death.** Patients die younger on average; the cause of death (for example suicide) can
  affect the brain transcriptome.
- **Lifespan signatures and our controls.** The lifespan atlas was built partly on HBCC controls [11], so these
  signatures are not independent of our controls.
- **Power.** With few donors per group in some cell types, the absence of an effect is not evidence of no effect; the
  direct SCZ vs BD test has even less power.
- **Choice of signatures.** We kept a few well-established hallmarks; others (oxidative stress, NAD+ and sirtuins,
  proteostasis and autophagy, nutrient sensing) were not tested.

**Perspective.** If an ageing-like profile driven by senescence or inflammaging were confirmed in some cell types, these
processes are already explored as therapeutic targets in other age-related diseases: senolytics, which remove senescent
cells, and senomorphics, which reduce their inflammatory secretions [13].

report); **supplementary** figures support them (appendix). To be confirmed with the real results.
